status_note: Block 1 of a multi-block handstand-walk arc. Tier A (never handstanded) through Tier D (walks 10m+, wants turns and obstacles). Multi-dimensional generation strategy: per-capability drill selection each session rather than a fixed weekly template. Dates in phases[] are template anchors from Mon 2026-01-05; the generator remaps to the user's real start date on activation.

goals.primary_intent: Build handstand-walk capability from the position you are actually in. Sub-capabilities (static hold, dynamic walk, turns, obstacles, wrist tolerance, shoulder endurance) train as independent state variables. Weekly plan targets your weakest measured capability first (Henry 1968; Proteau 1992).

arc.block_1_this_program: 8 weeks. Tier A builds wall-supported handstand hold + first freestand attempts. Tier B builds first freestanding hold + first walk step. Tier C builds 3-5 continuous steps. Tier D adds turns / obstacles / precision.
arc.block_2_expected: 8 weeks. Volume + skill breadth. Tier A → tier B graduation targeted. Tier D adds combined turns-in-walk.
arc.block_3_expected: 8-12 weeks. Consolidation and modality specificity (competition path or CrossFit metcon walk under fatigue).
arc.note: No cohort ETA — Ackerman 1988 and Wu 2014 both show 3-10× individual variance in psychomotor learning. The block gives you a personal delta, not a promise.

principles.rule: Static hold, dynamic walk, turns, obstacles are separate state variables — trained independently, not chained
principles.detail: Henry 1968 specificity + Newell 1985 constraints-led framework. A user who wall-holds 60s but can't take a step needs different drills from one who walks 8m but can't turn. The plan generator picks per-capability weakness each week.

principles.rule: Every drill card renders an external-focus cue by default (Wulf 1998, 2013)
principles.detail: External focus reliably outperforms internal focus for motor skill acquisition across ~100 studies. Cues direct attention to the environment or movement effect, never to body parts.

principles.rule: Video review is a button, not a schedule (Chiviacowsky & Wulf 2002, 2005)
principles.detail: Self-selected feedback outperforms forced schedules. The video review 'drill' surfaces after every skill set as optional — user taps if they want it, nothing shows automatically.

principles.rule: Blocked practice weeks 1-2, interleaved (contextual interference) from week 3
principles.detail: Wulf & Shea 2002 flag: CI benefit is smaller for complex real-world skills than lab tasks. Reduce challenge in acquisition, add later. Interleaving in the block phase means multiple drills per session in random order.

principles.rule: Daily short skill sessions beat infrequent long ones for handstand
principles.detail: Karni 1998 + Walker 2003 consolidation + Shea 2000 spacing. Skill demands frequent light exposure. 10-15 min of active handstand time × 4-6 days/week.

principles.rule: Any shoulder pain during a handstand attempt ends the session — no working through it
principles.detail: Pain during load consistently signals a compensation pattern that reinforces with continued exposure. Stop, review the video recording if made, restart next day. (General motor-learning principle; the specific handstand-shoulder biomechanics paper is flagged unverified — the rule survives on principle regardless.)

principles.rule: Weeks 1-2: wrist load ≤20-30 minutes/week. From week 3: increase ≤10%/week
principles.detail: Wiesinger 2019 tendon-adaptation timeframe. Explicitly an engineering choice: no direct wrist-load dose-response study exists. Vidal-Torija 2025 (n=321 adult practitioners): chronic wrist pain in 56.7%, no volume-hours association — risk is technique-driven, but the cap is a defensible upper bound.

questions.label: Realistically, how many days per week can you commit?
questions.help: Honest answer wins. If your ceiling is 2, we'll tell you upfront whether this program can deliver on its claim at that dose.

questions.label: How long can you hold a wall handstand (chest to wall or back to wall)?
How long can you freestand (no wall)?
How far can you handstand walk continuously?
Have you had wrist pain in the last 12 months during handstand or upper-body weight-bearing work?
Have you had shoulder pain during any overhead pressing or overhead hold in the last 12 months?
questions.help: Includes press, jerk, snatch, overhead squat, or any handstand attempt. If yes, we defer inversions this block and route the plan to shoulder-safe positions first.

options.hint: Barlow 2020: wrist WB tolerance drops from age 45 — extra ramp built in

questions.label: Have you been diagnosed with low bone density (osteoporosis or low BMD)?
questions.help: If yes, freestanding and any bail-risk attempts are contraindicated in this program. DiFiori 2006 catalogued distal radius as a common fracture site under this mechanism.

questions.label: Do you have high blood pressure that isn't under control? (Over 160/100 at rest, or diagnosed but not on medication — uncontrolled hypertension.)
questions.help: If yes, all inversions are deferred until BP is controlled — yoga-inversion literature documents transient systolic increases that stack with Valsalva during a kick-up.

questions.label: Do you have an acute wrist injury (sprain, TFCC, ligament tear) in the last 6 weeks?
questions.help: If yes, wrist-load drills are prohibited until cleared. The plan will offer hollow-body and shoulder-endurance drills only, with a note to clear with a clinician.

questions.label: If your handstand tips past vertical, what happens?
questions.help: Fear of falling gates handstand progress more than physical capacity for most self-taught users. Answer honestly — Phase 0 teaches this if you need it.

options.label: I'd fall onto my back or head
I can step or twist out but haven't drilled it
I can cartwheel or pirouette out reliably

questions.label: Concussion, or any dizziness / vertigo / balance disorder, in the last 3 months?
questions.help: This program trains inverted balance and opens with deliberate exits from a handstand.

questions.label: Are you pregnant?
questions.help: HR and BP responses shift in pregnancy, and inversion work is a conversation for your own clinician.

questions.label: I understand this program is a training template and not medical advice. I'll stop and see a clinician if wrist or shoulder pain persists after a session or if any bail results in a fall injury.

physical_tests.label: Passive wrist extension (degrees, painless)
physical_tests.instructions: Kneel with palms flat, fingertips pointing toward knees. Slowly rock weight forward until you feel a firm stretch — NOT pain. Estimate the wrist-extension angle. Target for Tier B+ is 70 degrees; Wiesinger 2019 mechanism basis for tendon load tolerance.

ranges.label: Barely bends back — under 45°
ranges.description: Fingertips lift off the floor when you rock forward, or you feel sharp discomfort early.

ranges.label: Some bend, no pain — about 60°
ranges.description: You can rock forward but the stretch stops you well before your wrist reaches vertical.

ranges.label: Reaches near vertical, mild stretch — about 75°
ranges.description: Wrist can pass through vertical with a firm but tolerable stretch.

ranges.label: Comfortable past vertical — 90°+
ranges.description: You can rock past vertical without discomfort. Tier B+ range.

physical_tests.label: Overhead shoulder flexion (degrees, standing)
physical_tests.instructions: Stand with your back to a wall, feet 15cm out. Keep low back flat. Raise both arms overhead as far as they go with elbows straight and thumbs pointing behind you. Target for Tier B+ is 170 degrees (engineering choice, mirroring weightlifting overhead pass-through cutoff).
physical_tests.video_search: shoulder flexion mobility test wall standing

ranges.label: Arms stop short — can't reach vertical
ranges.description: Arms stop 30° or more short of overhead when back stays flat on the wall.

ranges.label: Reaches vertical with effort
ranges.description: Arms brush the wall directly overhead but ribs pop or elbows bend to get there.

ranges.label: Reaches vertical, elbows straight, ribs stay down
ranges.description: Arms rest on the wall overhead with the low back still flat. Tier B+ range.

ranges.label: Passes behind vertical without effort
ranges.description: Arms sit slightly past the wall behind vertical.

physical_tests.label: Longest wall handstand hold, cold
physical_tests.instructions: Warm up wrists 2-3 min (rocking, finger raises). Kick or wall-walk into a chest-to-wall handstand. Hold to failure. Record seconds. Stop early if wrist or shoulder pain appears.

physical_tests.label: Longest freestand hold, cold (best of 5 attempts)
physical_tests.instructions: Warm up 3-5 min. Take up to 5 kick-up attempts and record the longest freestand hold. Zero counts if you can't hold at all. Do the attempts over a soft surface with a wall behind you.

physical_tests.label: Longest handstand walk distance, cold
physical_tests.instructions: If you can walk at all: mark a start line, kick up, walk as far as possible in one attempt. Record metres. Zero if no steps possible.

consent.label: I understand this is a training template, not medical advice. I'll consult a clinician for wrist or shoulder pain that persists past a session, or after any fall.
I agree to stop the session if shoulder pain appears during any handstand attempt — no training through it.

safety_gates.block_body: Freestanding handstands and bail landings load the distal radius and vertebrae — common fracture sites in osteoporosis. This program isn't safe to start without medical clearance.
Inversions transiently spike systolic pressure. Get hypertension controlled before adding inverted training.

safety_gates.block_title: Wait for the acute injury to resolve
safety_gates.block_body: An acute wrist injury needs healing time and clinical assessment. Come back once you're cleared to load the wrist.
Inverted balance training makes post-concussive and vestibular symptoms worse — that's our own guidance — and this program opens with deliberate falls. Come back once you've been cleared.

safety_gates.block_title: Talk to your clinician about inversion work
safety_gates.block_body: HR and BP responses shift in pregnancy, so heart-rate guidance here won't be reliable for you, and inverted work is a conversation to have with your midwife or clinician rather than with an app.
safety_gates.acknowledge_label: I've read this and I'll raise it with my clinician.

safety_gates.block_title: Worth knowing before you load the wrists
safety_gates.block_body: Most adults have never had a bone-density scan, so 'unsure' is the normal answer and we're not going to stop you. But weight-bearing on the hands is a wrist-loading programme — if you're post-menopausal, on long-term steroids, or have had a low-trauma fracture, ask your GP before Phase 1.
Being inverted raises blood pressure in the head and neck. A pharmacy cuff takes two minutes — get a reading before you start kicking up.
safety_gates.acknowledge_label: I'll get a reading before Phase 1.

safety_gates.block_title: Ramp the wrists, don't chase the calendar
safety_gates.block_body: Chronic wrist pain is common in this population — the survey we cite reports 56.7%. It's not a reason to stop you, but it is a reason to build wrist tolerance slowly, use parallettes or fists when the floor bites, and stop the session on sharp pain rather than working through it.
safety_gates.acknowledge_label: Understood — I'll ramp and stop on sharp pain.

safety_gates.block_title: Worth being certain before you go upside down
safety_gates.block_body: If you've had a head knock and aren't sure whether it settled, find out before training inverted balance. Lingering dizziness or visual disturbance in an inversion is how people land badly.
safety_gates.acknowledge_label: Understood — I'll stop and get checked if anything spins.

plan_tiers.label: Tier A — Foundation (no handstand yet)
plan_tiers.typical_outcome: By week 8: stable Kinoshita position 3 hold, first assisted wall handstand hold of 10-20 seconds, and 2-3 wall walks in a session without wrist symptoms.

program_adjustments.note: Foundation tier is a 4-session/week, 12-minute-per-session load. Kinoshita position ladder + wrist prep dominate weeks 1-3. First wall-walk lands week 2. First chest-to-wall hold attempt week 4. No freestand attempts this block.

plan_tiers.label: Tier B — Wall handstand established
plan_tiers.typical_outcome: By week 8: first 5-15 second freestand hold, first walk attempts on the wall, wall handstand hold up to 45-60 seconds.

program_adjustments.note: Reference tier. Weekly template runs as written. Wall-supported balance-search (belly-to-wall) starts week 1, freestand attempts staged in from week 3.

plan_tiers.label: Tier C — Freestanding, learning to walk
plan_tiers.typical_outcome: By week 8: 3-5 continuous handstand walk steps, freestand hold pushed to 15-25 seconds, first short shuttles chained.

program_adjustments.note: Single-step attempts and 2-3-step shuttles dominate. Freestand hold retested weekly (KPI). Wall shoulder taps as a bridge drill in week 1-2.

plan_tiers.label: Tier D — Advanced (walks 10m+, wants turns / obstacles)
plan_tiers.typical_outcome: By week 8: first clean 180 pirouette OR first traverse over a 5kg plate OR consistent narrow-lane precision path. Continuous walk distance extended by 20-40%.

program_adjustments.note: Variability + obstacles dominate. Turns on wall week 1, first free half-pirouette attempts week 4+. Plate traversal from week 3. User self-selects turn vs obstacle emphasis at intake question (implicit via which capability is weakest).

program_goal.unit: z-score composite of hold + walk + wrist tolerance

phases.name: Week 0 — Exits before line
phases.goal: Learn to fall on purpose before you learn to hold vertical. Fear-of-falling gates handstand progress more than physical capacity for most self-taught users.
phases.rationale: Fear-of-falling literature: Adkin & Frank 2000/2002 (postural threat alters muscle activation before the fall); Carpenter 2001 (anxiety degrades balance strategy); Hardy 1996 catastrophe model (anxiety above threshold causes performance collapse, not linear degradation); Bandura (mastery experiences on bail-outs reduce threat perception on the primary skill — you don't reduce fear by walking more). Gymnastics/circus pedagogy (USA Gymnastics, NICA, Emmet Louis, Yuval Ayalon) treats cartwheel exit / pirouette / tuck forward roll as pre-requisite to freestanding, not optional. Phase 0 is deliberately short — one week of exit drills, not a rehab arc.

criteria_any: coach_or_video_evidence: successful pirouette exit or cartwheel exit demonstrated
retest_gate.on_success: Advance to phase_1_foundation_prep. bail_out_confidence remains a daily log field the engine consults.
retest_gate.on_fail: Repeat Phase 0 for another week. If fear persists >2 weeks, the intake nudges the user to work with a coach for 1-2 sessions — this is the pattern that reliably breaks the fear cycle (see rationale).

phases.name: Weeks 1-2 — Wrist prep + Kinoshita position ladder (blocked practice)
phases.goal: Build wrist load tolerance base + first exposure to the Kinoshita position 1 and 2 holds. No wall handstand attempts yet for Tier A.
phases.template_note: Blocked practice (Shea & Morgan 1979, Wulf & Shea 2002): one drill focus per session. Reduces cognitive load in acquisition.
notes: Wrist prep is not optional — 3-5 min every session (Wiesinger 2019 tendon-adaptation window).
Weekly wrist volume cap: ≤30 min total in this phase. Engine tracks and warns if exceeded.

phases.name: Weeks 1-4 — Wall handstand established + first freestand attempts
phases.goal: Consolidate the wall handstand shape, add balance-search (belly-to-wall), begin freestand kick-up attempts from week 3.
phases.template_note: Week 1-2 blocked, week 3+ interleaves wall hold + freestand attempt in the same session.
notes: Video review button available after every freestand attempt — self-selected (Chiviacowsky & Wulf 2002).
Wall hold KPI: seconds, tracked weekly.

phases.name: Weeks 1-4 — Single steps + short shuttles
phases.goal: Extend freestand hold to 15+ seconds and chain first walking steps. Yiou 2017 CoP-shift work informs the single-step drill order.
phases.template_note: Freestand hold and walk-step drills interleaved from week 1 (CI benefit expected because user is past cognitive stage). Wall shoulder taps as bridge from week 1.
notes: Walk KPI: continuous steps per attempt, best of 5.
Wrist symptom score (0-10, next-morning) tracked daily.

phases.name: Weeks 1-8 — Variability, turns, obstacles
phases.goal: Add turns and obstacles. Week 1-2 wall pirouette + plate walkover attempts. Week 3+ first freestanding pirouette attempts.
phases.template_note: Fully interleaved (random CI) from week 1 — Tier D users past the cognitive stage. Multi-drill sessions.
notes: Advanced tier: user self-selects turns vs obstacle emphasis by which capability_domain is weakest.

phases.name: Weeks 3-8 — Interleaved practice for all tiers (post-acquisition)
phases.goal: Once weeks 1-2 blocked-practice acquisition is complete, interleave. Plan generator picks 2-3 drills per session across the user's weakest capabilities.
phases.template_note: Multi-dimensional generator picks from the drill_library filtered by the user's capability_profile. Weakest capability first (Henry 1968, Proteau 1992).
phases.test_at_end: Week 8: full re-assessment (wall hold, freestand, walk distance, wrist symptom score, wrist extension mobility).
notes: Weekly retest: freestand hold time (single metric, cheap).

blocks.name: Wrist prep — every session
blocks.note: 3-5 min of wrist prep + finger raises before any load-bearing drill. Weekly wrist volume cap: 20-30 min weeks 1-2, +≤10%/week thereafter (Wiesinger 2019 mechanism basis; engineering choice on exact numbers).

blocks.name: Skill session A — Kinoshita position ladder
blocks.note: Kinoshita position ladder — progressive shoulder overhead endurance without full inversion.

blocks.name: Skill session A — wall handstand hold + shrugs (Tier A/B)
blocks.note: Chest-to-wall hold as primary; belly-to-wall added when user reaches level 2 in handstand_hold_static.

blocks.name: Skill session B — kick-up + freestand attempts (Tier B)
blocks.note: Kick-up practice + freestand hold attempts. Video review button available after each set (Chiviacowsky & Wulf 2002 self-selected KP).

items.note: User taps to review a recorded attempt. Never auto-shown.

blocks.name: Skill session A — freestand hold (Tier C)
blocks.note: Freestand hold time is the primary KPI (weekly). Tuck freestand for reduced moment of inertia when hunting first extended holds.

blocks.name: Skill session B — single-step walks + shuttles (Tier C)
blocks.note: Single-step attempts as primary skill focus. Short shuttles (Shea & Morgan 1979 + spacing) beat one big continuous attempt.

blocks.name: Skill session A — variability walks (Tier D)
blocks.note: Line + markers + precision-lane walks. Variability of practice (Schmidt 1975 schema theory).

blocks.name: Skill session B — obstacles or turns (Tier D, weakest-first)
blocks.note: Generator picks obstacles OR turns based on which capability_domain the user is weakest in. Both progressive: wall pirouette → free pirouette; plate walkover → cones → precision.

blocks.name: Wrist + shoulder recovery flush
blocks.note: Post-session recovery: down-dog / child's pose wrist stretches. 3-5 min, non-optional in weeks 1-3 while wrist load tolerance is being built.

blocks.name: Wall cartwheel exit
blocks.note: The single most-used bail-out for over-tipping. Start from a controlled wall handstand, drop one arm, rotate hips, land on that side's leg. Fail forward, not backward.
blocks.rationale: Standard gymnastics/circus exit taught pre-freestanding. Once the pattern is automatic, over-tipping stops feeling terrifying because the body knows the exit.

blocks.name: Quarter-turn pirouette from wall
blocks.note: From wall handstand, twist upper body 90° and step down to feet. Practices the escape route to the SIDE when a straight-back cartwheel isn't available.
blocks.rationale: Wulf 2013 external focus: cue is 'point your chest at the wall' — external target reduces anxiety. Wraps hip rotation into a bail pattern the user can use even when tired.

blocks.name: Tuck forward roll from crow
blocks.note: From a crow pose, tuck chin, roll forward onto upper back, come up to sitting. Teaches the FORWARD escape route — the one people usually don't have.
blocks.rationale: Provides a redundant escape (in addition to cartwheel + pirouette). Users with only-cartwheel-out often panic when the tip goes forward instead of sideways. Roll trains the forward option.

blocks.name: Deliberate mat falls with breath control
blocks.note: From wall handstand, LET GO ON PURPOSE. Land on mat (crash mat if available, thick yoga mat OK). Exhale on impact. Do this cold — the body needs to prove to itself that a controlled fall is a survivable non-event.
blocks.rationale: Bandura self-efficacy: mastery experiences on the feared thing (the fall itself) reduce threat perception. The exhale cue borrows from paratrooper training — passive-exhale-on-impact is the anti-freeze response.

weekly_template.note: Multi-dimensional generation: the generator picks 2-3 drills per session at composition time based on the user's capability_profile. This template is a slot layout only — it declares WHEN sessions happen and their type, not which drills. The multi_dimensional branch of plan-generator.ts fills the drills per session.
placement_principles: Consecutive skill sessions OK — daily short beats infrequent long for skill (Karni 1998, Walker 2003).
Wrist prep before every session. Recovery flush after every session. Non-negotiable in weeks 1-3.
48h clear between any hard shoulder-loaded session (kick-up practice) and heavy pressing / pulling elsewhere in your training.
If you miss a session, don't double up — spacing benefit is lost by cramming (Shea 2000).
Robertson 2004 consolidation window: 4-6h post-practice is vulnerable to similar-task interference. Don't do a handstand session immediately after a heavy overhead press session.

progression_rules.assessment_note: Judge by next-morning wrist symptom score + subjective recovery. Video review of best attempt is optional feedback (self-controlled).

states.label: Proceed as written — engine picks weakest capability, generator composes session
Hold — engine reduces the wrist-load drills, keeps the shoulder-endurance drills

conditions.or: life_load 7+ or sleep < 6h two nights running

states.label: Skip today's session or do wrist recovery + hollow body only

progression_rules.week_end_rule: If the week's freestand-hold retest improved OR wrist symptom score trended down → advance capability_profile.estimated_level where applicable. If freestand hold regressed AND wrist symptom score elevated → hold the level; engine picks lower-level drills next week.
progression_rules.escalation: Two red days in a week → skip the higher-load skill session (kick-up or walk attempts) that week, replace with Kinoshita position 1 and hollow-body only. Persistent shoulder pain > 3 days → stop, see a clinician. Pain-during-load motor-learning principle: continued exposure with pain reinforces the compensation pattern.

daily_log_schema.derived_state_rule: red if wrist_symptom_score > 6 OR shoulder_symptom_score > 3 OR new_acute_injury; amber if wrist_symptom_score 4-6 OR life_load >= 7; else green If bail_out_confidence <= 3, the day defers walking attempts to wall-supported holds regardless of symptom score.

bail_out_confidence.label: Bail-out confidence today
bail_out_confidence.hint: How confident are you that you can exit an over-tipped handstand safely if it goes wrong right now? 0 = 'terrified', 10 = 'certain'. Low scores gate the engine off walking attempts today.

immediate_actions.action: Complete the intake questionnaire and 5 physical tests within 3 days of starting.
immediate_actions.reason: Tier assignment and capability_profile seeding depend on all five test values. Missing a value defaults it to the tier floor, which may under-load an advanced user.

immediate_actions.action: Set up a phone stand or ask a partner to occasionally record you — video review is a KPI and a feedback tool.
immediate_actions.reason: Chiviacowsky & Wulf 2002: self-controlled feedback outperforms forced schedules. The video review button only works if a clip exists.

immediate_actions.action: Read the shoulder-pain-stops-session rule and agree to it.
immediate_actions.reason: Pain-during-load motor-learning principle: continued exposure with pain reinforces the compensation pattern. Non-negotiable.

immediate_actions.action: Establish a soft-landing zone — mat, grass, or floor with a clear kick-out lane.
immediate_actions.reason: Freestand attempts have a bail probability. DiFiori 2006 catalogued the fracture sites; a soft floor and a clear bail path mitigate the mechanism.

physiological_targets: Wrist load tolerance — tendon adaptation timeframe roughly 8-12 weeks for early collagen turnover (Wiesinger 2019 — used as mechanism basis; no direct dose-response for handstand wrist load, flagged as engineering choice). Vidal-Torija 2025 (n=321 adult practitioners): 56.7% report chronic wrist pain but NO association with weekly training hours — technique-driven, not volume-driven. Barlow 2020: adult wrist WB tolerance declines from age 45.

Shoulder overhead endurance — sustained flexion at ≥170° draws on serratus anterior, upper/lower trapezius endurance (Ludewig & Cook 2000 shoulder-impingement kinematics; Ludewig & Reynolds 2009). Sadowski 2021: a straight-arm press to handstand produces ~3× BW shoulder moment — do NOT program straight-arm press early.

Balance strategy — the handstand hold is wrist-torque-dominated (Kerwin & Trewartha 2001; Blenkinsop 2017). Elite vs novice differ mainly in medial-lateral CoP control + stiffening strategy (Sobera 2019; Baker 2025 systematic review). Novices show a wider CoP excursion; training reduces variability with time.

Progressive position ladder — Kinoshita 2022 EMG-validated the 4-position progression: 90° incline → 135° incline → elbow / straddle-L stand → full wall handstand. Each step approximately doubles the overhead time-under-tension.

Motor consolidation — Karni 1998 (fast/slow learning phases, M1 remapping over ~3 weeks); Walker 2003 (dissociable consolidation stages); Robertson 2004 (4-6h post-practice interference window). Daily short skill exposure builds a stronger trace than infrequent long sessions.

Feedback — Chiviacowsky & Wulf 2002, 2005: self-controlled feedback beats forced schedules. Potdevin 2018 (n=18 children, 8-week gymnastics): video KP after ~5 reps improved skill AND self-assessment. Rohleder & Vogt 2018: combined tactile-verbal + visual feedback outperforms either alone.

External focus — Wulf 1998, 2013 (15-year review, ~100 studies): external focus reliably outperforms internal focus across balance and complex motor skills. McNevin 2003: farther external targets amplify the effect. Wulf & Lewthwaite 2016 OPTIMAL theory: external focus + enhanced expectancies + autonomy compound.

session_rationale.block_wrist_prep: Wrist tissue adaptation lags most other adaptations by weeks (Wiesinger 2019). 3-5 min of graded wrist prep before every session builds accumulated exposure without spiking a single session. Vidal-Torija 2025 shows chronic pain is technique-driven, not volume-driven — but the volume cap is a defensible upper bound while good technique is being built. Weekly cap 20-30 min in weeks 1-2 is an engineering choice (no direct dose-response study).
session_rationale.block_skill_A_kinoshita: Kinoshita 2022 progressive position ladder: 90° incline hold recruits the shoulder overhead endurance system without asking for full balance. EMG-validated. Ideal Tier A entry point — the shape of a handstand loaded through the same tissues, with no bail risk. Sadowski 2021 explains why straight-arm press to handstand is NOT a Tier A drill: 3× BW shoulder moment is too much, too early.
session_rationale.block_skill_A_wall_hold: Chest-to-wall hold builds the plumb-line shape under load (Kerwin & Trewartha 2001 wrist-strategy characterisation). Wall shrugs isolate the serratus / trap endurance that a handstand demands over time (Ludewig & Cook 2000). Belly-to-wall added when static hold is level 2: introduces active wrist strategy that a chest-to-wall hold hides.
session_rationale.block_skill_B_freestand_search: Kick-up practice + freestand attempts + optional tuck freestand for reduced moment of inertia. Video review button is self-controlled (Chiviacowsky & Wulf 2002) — user taps if they want feedback, no auto-show. Potdevin 2018 pattern: KP after ~5 reps, not every rep.
session_rationale.block_skill_A_freestand_hold: Freestand hold is the primary KPI at Tier C — trackable weekly, sensitive early indicator. Sobera 2019: elite-novice CoP-variability differences mean the freestand hold time is a valid capability marker across the skill acquisition arc.
session_rationale.block_skill_B_walk_attempts: Single-step attempts + 2-3-step shuttles. Yiou 2017 walking-initiation biomechanics: the CoP shift precedes the step. Short shuttles beat one long attempt — Shea & Morgan 1979 CI + spacing effect + Shea 2000 spaced practice.
session_rationale.block_skill_A_variability: Line + markers + precision-lane walks train variability of practice (Schmidt 1975 schema theory; Wulf & Shea 2002 constant→variable progression). Tier D users are past the cognitive stage; variable practice benefits are largest here.
session_rationale.block_skill_B_obstacles_or_turns: Weakest-capability priority (Henry 1968; Proteau 1992). Generator picks turns vs obstacles based on which capability_domain has the lower estimated_level. Progressive gate: wall pirouette level 4 → free half-pirouette; free half → full pirouette. Plate → cones → narrow lane.
session_rationale.block_recovery: Down-dog + child's pose wrist decompression. Vidal-Torija 2025: chronic wrist pain is technique-driven — a decompression flush is not a fix for bad technique, but paired with the video-review button it drives the user to notice + correct.

evidence_base.progression_rationale: Weeks 1-2 are blocked practice per Wulf & Shea 2002 — the crucial caveat that simple-lab CI benefits often reverse in complex real-world skills; reduce challenge in acquisition, add it in retention. From week 3 the multi-dimensional generator interleaves 2-3 drills per session across the user's weakest capabilities (Henry 1968, Proteau 1992 specificity). Tier assignment at intake seeds capability_profile.estimated_level per capability_domain; the generator picks drills whose level matches the user's current level per domain, filtered by prerequisites. Weekly freestand-hold retest is the cheapest KPI — a single number, sensitive to daily consolidation (Walker 2003). Full re-assessment at 4 and 8 weeks re-seeds the capability_profile. Wrist-load progression is capped: 20-30 min weeks 1-2, then ≤10%/week — explicitly an engineering choice, not evidence, but respects Wiesinger 2019 tendon-adaptation timeframe. Tier D users skip the blocked weeks (already past acquisition) and enter interleaved from week 1.
evidence_base.outcome_evidence: No cohort ETAs — Ackerman 1988 (early-stage cognitive ability correlates), Wu 2014 (3× variance in visuomotor rotation learning, baseline motor variability predicts). Realistic 8-week Block 1 outcomes: Tier A — stable Kinoshita 3-4 hold, first assisted wall hold, no freestand yet. Tier B — first 5-15s freestand hold, first wall pirouettes. Tier C — 3-5 continuous walk steps, extended by short shuttles. Tier D — first pirouette OR obstacle traverse OR precision-path work; walk distance +20-40%. These match coach-consensus corroborated ranges. Voelcker-Rehage & Willimczik 2006: older adults learn slower but retention plateau is similar — the 46-60+ age bands may take an extra 2-4 weeks to reach the Tier's typical outcome but the endpoint is comparable. Macnamara 2014 meta on deliberate practice: sport variance explained is 18% — 82% is not deliberate practice. Do not sell 10,000 hours; the honest promise is 'consistent, targeted, spaced short sessions reliably move each sub-capability'.

tier_b_wall_handstand.walk_target: first wall-walk pirouette + first free steps

tier_d_advanced.turn_target: first 180 pirouette OR obstacle traverse OR precision path

contraindications: Shoulder pain during a handstand attempt — session ends immediately. Do not train through it. Pain-during-load motor-learning principle: continued exposure with pain reinforces a compensation pattern.

Osteoporosis diagnosis (or low-BMD DEXA) — freestanding and any bail-risk attempts contraindicated. DiFiori 2006 catalogued distal radius as a common fracture site under this mechanism; vertebral and hip fractures follow. Tier A wall walks + Kinoshita positions with a spotter and soft floor are permitted only after clinician clearance.

Uncontrolled hypertension (BP > 160/100 at rest or unmedicated) — defer all inversions until BP is controlled. Yoga-inversion literature documents transient systolic increases that stack with Valsalva during a kick-up attempt.

Acute wrist injury (sprain, TFCC tear, ligament instability) in the last 6 weeks — wrist-load drills prohibited until cleared by a clinician. Program will offer hollow-body and shoulder-endurance drills only during this window.

Persistent shoulder impingement or rotator-cuff pathology — sustained overhead position at ≥170° is not safe. Ludewig & Cook 2000, Reinold 2007: modified overhead loading and scapular retraining first, defer this program.
First-trimester pregnancy — HR and BP responses shift; inversion literature is unclear. Defer.
Recent concussion or vestibular disorder — inverted balance training exacerbates symptoms.
evidence_base.adaptive_engine_hooks: Wrist symptom score is the primary daily signal. Score > 6 for a day → gate the next session to recovery only (skip kick-up + walk attempts). Score 4-6 → engine proposes swapping wrist-load-heavy drills for wall-supported holds (proposal, user Accepts). Shoulder pain report → session immediately routes to non-inverted mobility + hollow body; multi-day persistence flags the user to see a clinician. Weekly freestand-hold retest: two consecutive weeks with a regression AND wrist symptom score up → engine drops the user's handstand_hold_static level by 1 and picks lower-level drills next week. Video review self-select frequency is tracked (motivation proxy per Chiviacowsky & Wulf) but doesn't gate anything. Tier D obstacles-vs-turns emphasis is auto-picked by which capability_domain is weakest at composition time. All engine adjustments respect the confirm-first rule — engine proposes, user Accepts, nothing mutates silently.
engineering_choices_flagged: 20-30 min/week wrist volume cap in weeks 1-2 — mechanism basis in Wiesinger 2019, no direct dose-response study for handstand wrist load. Defensible upper bound, not evidence.
≤10%/week wrist-volume increment after week 2 — mirrors Gabbett 2016 acute-to-chronic workload heuristic. Not directly tested for handstand.
170° shoulder flexion prerequisite for Tier B+ — analogous to weightlifting overhead pass-through cutoff, not empirically validated for handstand.

60s wall hold as a soft gate before freestand attempts — coach folklore, no RCT. Program uses freestand_hold_max_seconds directly from the physical test, not the wall hold, to seed the freestand-attempt drills.
15s freestand as pirouette gate — no evidence. Program uses handstand_turns_level explicitly, not seconds.
5-drill freestand set count, 30s attempt cap — spacing-derived, not directly tested.
4-6 sessions per week — daily-short-beats-long inference from Karni 1998 + Walker 2003 + Shea 2000. No direct handstand-frequency RCT.
10-18 min per session — engineering choice matching adult recreational-practitioner attention span. Not dose-response validated.
Blocked practice weeks 1-2 threshold — Wulf & Shea 2002 supports blocked in acquisition but doesn't specify the exact week to switch. Two-week floor is pragmatic.
Tier D self-selection of obstacles vs turns via weakest-capability rule — theoretically supported by Henry 1968 / Proteau 1992 but not directly RCT'd.

Weakest-capability-first drill selection across all tiers — the engine biases each session toward the user's lowest-scoring sub-skill (wrist load, hollow-shape, turns, obstacle nav, etc.). This is coaching-consensus, theoretically supported by specificity of adaptation but not RCT-validated at the sub-skill granularity we operate at.

references.title: Progressive four-position handstand EMG activity
references.used_for: The 4-position progression ladder (90° incline → 135° → elbow / straddle-L → full wall handstand). Validated by EMG activity of shoulder / core musculature. Underpins block_skill_A_kinoshita and the Tier A entry. Flagged for founder review: DOI missing.

references.title: Strategies for maintaining a handstand in the anterior-posterior direction
references.source: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise 33(7):1182-1188
references.used_for: Wrist-torque-dominated balance strategy (analogous to ankle strategy in upright stance). Underpins the fingertip-tap drill and belly-to-wall balance-search rationale.

references.authors: Blenkinsop GM, Pain MTG, Hiley MJ
references.title: Balance control strategies during perturbed and unperturbed balance in standing and handstand
references.used_for: Confirms wrist-strategy dominance under perturbation. Used in physiological_targets and freestand-attempt drill rationale.

references.authors: Sobera M, Serafin R, Rutkowska-Kucharska A
references.title: Postural control strategies of handstand-trained subjects
references.used_for: Elite vs novice difference — medial-lateral CoP control + stiffening strategy. Used in outcome_evidence and freestand hold rationale.

references.authors: MacDonald C, Baker JS, Gu Y, Ugbolue UC
references.title: A systematic review of the biomechanics of the handstand
references.source: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living (PMC12745452), 21 studies 1988-2025
references.used_for: Current best synthesis of handstand biomechanics — wrist strategy, elite-novice CoP differences, thin evidence base for prerequisite thresholds. Anchor citation for the whole evidence_base.

references.title: Combined tactile-verbal and visual feedback in gymnastics skill acquisition
references.source: Science of Gymnastics Journal / International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport 18(1)
references.used_for: Combined tactile-verbal + visual feedback outperforms either alone. Used in feedback_type rationale and video_review drill design.

references.title: Video feedback and self-assessment in gymnastics learning
references.used_for: n=18 children, 8-week gymnastics: video KP after ~5 reps improved skill and self-assessment. Used in block_skill_B_freestand_search rationale and video_review dosing (not every rep).

references.title: Self-controlled feedback: does it enhance learning because performers get feedback when they need it?
references.source: Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport 73:408-415
references.used_for: Self-controlled feedback beats forced schedules. The video review button design (self-selected, never auto-shown) is directly from this study.

references.title: Kinematic and kinetic analysis of the straight-arm press to handstand
references.used_for: Shoulder-moment analysis of the press to handstand. Directly informs the choice NOT to program straight-arm press early, and the Tier A entry at Kinoshita 90°. Attribution flagged for founder review (see citations.json review_note): DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0253951 resolves to a Mizutori-authored parallel-bars paper. The heavy-shoulder-moment principle survives on general grounds; the specific 3× BW figure was a parallel-bars finding, not a floor finding — do not cite that number.

references.authors: Barlow C, Scholtz K, Medeiros DM
references.title: Adult wrist weight-bearing tolerance across the lifespan
references.source: Journal of Hand Therapy (n=465 healthy adults)
references.used_for: Wrist WB tolerance declines from age 45. Informs the age-band intake question and Tier B+ warm-up ramp for older users.

references.title: Wrist symptoms in adult handstand practitioners: a cross-sectional survey
references.used_for: 56.7% chronic wrist pain but NO association with weekly training hours, frequency, warm-up, or brace use. Reframes wrist risk as technique-driven, not volume-driven — but supports the volume cap as a conservative upper bound. Attribution flagged for founder review: PMC12550924 resolves to Martonovich et al. (same underlying data). The claim itself survives; the author byline may need to be swapped.

references.authors: DiFiori JP, Caine DJ, Malina RM
references.title: Wrist pain, distal radial physeal injury, and ulnar variance in the young gymnast
references.used_for: Fracture-site data at distal radius under load-through-hand mechanism. Cohort is young gymnasts (open physes); Terav uses this as a mechanism analog for the adult low-BMD osteoporosis contraindication, not as direct evidence in adult practitioners.

references.title: Tendon adaptation to mechanical loading
references.used_for: Tendon adaptation timeframe (8-12 weeks for collagen turnover). Mechanism basis for the wrist volume cap. Note: no direct dose-response study for handstand wrist load — the exact 20-30 min cap is an engineering choice. Flagged for founder review: DOI missing.

references.title: Alterations in shoulder kinematics and associated muscle activity in people with symptoms of shoulder impingement
references.used_for: Serratus + trapezius endurance in sustained overhead flexion. Underpins the wall_supported_shrugs drill and the 170° prerequisite.

references.title: Electromyographic analysis of the supraspinatus and deltoid muscles during 3 common rehabilitation exercises
references.source: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
references.used_for: Rotator cuff / deltoid activation patterns in overhead loading. Cited in shoulder-endurance contraindication and belly-to-wall hold rationale.

references.title: The acquisition of skilled motor performance: fast and slow experience-driven changes in primary motor cortex
references.used_for: Fast (within-session) vs slow (across-session) motor learning. M1 remapping over ~3 weeks. Underpins the daily-short-sessions design.

references.authors: Walker MP, Brakefield T, Hobson JA, Stickgold R
references.title: Dissociable stages of human memory consolidation and reconsolidation
references.used_for: Sleep-dependent motor consolidation. Reinforces daily-short skill exposure over infrequent long sessions. Journal + byline corrected 2026-08-17 — canonical entry in citations.json is now Learning & Memory 10(4):275-284 (matches whitepaper 04).

references.title: Contextual interference effects on the acquisition, retention, and transfer of a motor skill
references.source: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory 5:179-187
references.used_for: Foundational contextual-interference paper: blocked better in acquisition, random better in retention. Underpins the weeks-1-2-blocked / weeks-3+-interleaved progression.

references.authors: Sci Reports handstand-walk shoulder pain team
references.title: Handstand walking biomechanics and shoulder pain association
references.used_for: Pain-associated practitioners show a technique-driven compensation pattern. Underpins the non-negotiable 'shoulder pain stops session' rule. Byline and DOI checked against the publisher record on 2026-09-02.

references.authors: Yiou E, Caderby T, Delafontaine A, Fourcade P, Honeine JL
references.title: Balance control during gait initiation: State-of-the-art and research perspectives
references.used_for: Walking initiation biomechanics — CoP shift precedes step. Informs the single_step_attempt drill design and the 'lean the shape toward the far wall' external-focus cue. Replaced ferrari_2021 (unlocatable) 2026-08-18 per founder-approved plan.

references.title: Upper-quadrant Y-balance and CKCUEST vs handstand E-score
references.used_for: UQYBT/CKCUEST show NO predictive relationship with handstand E-score. Used to justify NOT gating obstacles / turns on generic upper-quadrant screens, and to reinforce sub-skill-independence principle.

references.authors: Wulf G, Höß M, Prinz W
references.title: Instructions for motor learning: differential effects of internal versus external focus of attention
references.used_for: External focus outperforms internal focus. Foundational reference for the cues_external_focus field on every drill.

references.title: Attentional focus and motor learning: a review of 15 years
references.source: International Review of Sport and Exercise Psychology 6:77-104
references.used_for: 15-year review of ~100 studies confirming external focus benefit. Codified in the external_focus_default principle.

references.title: Principles derived from the study of simple skills do not generalize to complex skill learning
references.used_for: The crucial caveat that CI benefits are smaller for complex skills. Underpins the blocked-first, interleaved-later progression.

references.title: Specificity vs generality in learning motor skill
references.used_for: Specificity hypothesis: motor abilities are task-specific. Underpins the sub-skill-independence principle and the multi_dimensional generation strategy itself.

references.authors: Proteau L, Marteniuk RG, Lévesque L
references.title: Learning is specific to the sensory conditions of practice
references.used_for: Specificity of practice — learning is bound to the sensory context. Underpins the choice to train wall hold + freestand + walk as separate state variables.

references.title: Coordination, control, and skill: constraints-led framework
references.used_for: Organismic, task, environmental constraints. Underpins the multi-dimensional decomposition into capability_domains.

references.title: Practice spacing effects on motor skill acquisition and retention
references.used_for: Spacing across days > massing within a day. Underpins daily-short design and the 'don't double up if you miss a session' rule.

references.authors: Robertson EM, Pascual-Leone A, Miall RC
references.title: Current concepts in procedural consolidation
references.used_for: 4-6h post-practice consolidation window vulnerable to similar-task interference. Underpins the 'don't stack handstand practice immediately after heavy overhead press' placement rule.

references.title: A schema theory of discrete motor skill learning
references.used_for: Schema theory — variability builds recall + recognition schemas. Underpins the variability-of-practice at Tier D (line, markers, precision lane).

references.title: Injury prevention in women's gymnastics
references.used_for: Skill-readiness assessment as injury mitigation. Cited in prerequisite gating on advanced drills.

references.title: Determinants of individual differences during skill acquisition
references.used_for: Individual variance in psychomotor learning. Underpins 'no cohort ETA' in outcome_evidence.

references.title: Temporal structure of motor variability is dynamically regulated and predicts motor learning ability
references.used_for: 3× variance in visuomotor rotation learning correlates with baseline motor variability. Reinforces individual-variance framing.

would_additionally_use.label: Per-drill quality tag
would_additionally_use.why_it_matters: A drill logged as 'done' could be clean or shaky — the engine treats both the same. A quality tag lets the engine trust progression rather than just count reps.
would_additionally_use.user_action_free: Tag each drill session as clean / shaky / assisted after finishing.

would_additionally_use.label: Weekly retest on schedule
would_additionally_use.why_it_matters: Skill drift is invisible without a fixed retest. Skipping retest weeks means the engine can't tell if you're advancing or regressing.
would_additionally_use.user_action_free: Do the weekly retest of the tier gate on the day the plan schedules it.
